questions.q: What is the primary role of a protagonist in a short story, and how does Sherlock Holmes fulfill this role in "The Adventure of the Three Garridebs"?
questions.a: The protagonist is the central character who drives the plot forward through their actions and decisions. In this story, Sherlock Holmes is the protagonist because he initiates the investigation, uncovers the fraud, and orchestrates the capture of Killer Evans. A wrong answer might name Nathan Garrideb as the protagonist because the title mentions "Three Garridebs," revealing a misunderstanding that the title character is always the protagonist.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how Holmes's "digressions" (like noting the cut of the coat or the house-agent) contribute to solving the case, rather than being irrelevant chatter.
questions.a: Holmes's digressions are deliberate information-gathering tactics: the coat/boots reveal the American's true residence in London, and the house-agent visit confirms the previous tenant was the murdered forger Presbury. A wrong answer would say Holmes was just showing off or being rude, missing that every "irrelevant" detail builds his hypothesis about the criminal's identity and motive.

questions.q: Apply the PEEL method to analyze one trait of Holmes (e.g., his observational skill) using a specific moment from the text. Write a complete PEEL paragraph.
questions.a: Point: Holmes possesses extraordinary observational skills. Evidence: He deduces the American lawyer has lived in London long-term from "the shoulder cut of your coat, the toes of your boots." Explanation: This shows Holmes reads minute material details to expose lies, a core method. Link: This observation initiates the unraveling of the Garrideb fraud. A poor answer might quote the line but not explain how it reveals character or advance the argument.

questions.q: Compare Holmes's professional detachment in the first half of the story with his emotional reaction when Watson is wounded. What does this contrast reveal about his character?
questions.a: The contrast reveals Holmes's humanity beneath his analytical exterior: his "cold mask" hides deep loyalty and love for Watson, showing intellect and emotion are not mutually exclusive. A wrong answer would treat the two sides as contradictory or say Holmes only cares about the case, ignoring the text's explicit statement: "It was worth a wound... to know the depth of loyalty and love which lay behind that cold mask."

questions.q: Evaluate whether Holmes's decision to let the American lawyer go to Birmingham (instead of arresting him immediately) was a tactical brilliance or an unnecessary risk. Justify with textual evidence.
questions.a: It was tactical brilliance: Holmes says "it seemed better to clear the stage by letting him go" to catch him in the act at the secret cellar, preserving evidence and ensuring a conviction. A weak evaluation would call it reckless because Evans shot Watson, overlooking that Holmes anticipated danger ("If our Wild West friend tries to live up to his nickname, we must be ready") and had revolvers ready.

questions.q: Create a brief diary entry from Holmes's perspective on the night before the Ryder Street adventure, reflecting on the case and his concern for Watson. Use at least two character traits revealed in the story.
questions.a: A strong entry would show Holmes's analytical mind reviewing the evidence (the misspelled advertisement, the house-agent's information) and his concealed affection for Watson ("I should know my Watson by now... it will only be an additional reason to you for running your head into danger"). A poor entry would make Holmes sound overly emotional or ignore his deductive process.
